newsitem.title: CHINA: HANG SENG BANK SEES HK GROWING 5.4 PCT IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: HANG SENG BANK SEES HK GROWING 5.4 PCT IN 1997.

text.p: Hang Seng Bank has maintained its forecast for a 5.4 percent 1997 growth rate for Hong Kong in its mid-year economic review of the territory, but reduced its inflation outlook to 6.5 percent from 7.0 percent.

"Underpinned by sustained growth in consumer and investment spending, the local economy is expected to attain GDP (gross domestic product) growth of 5.4 percent in 1997," Hang Seng Bank said in a report.
Despite the expanding economy, the bank revised downward its inflation forecast as a result of a drop in import prices helped by a strong Hong Kong dollar.

Hang Seng Bank said domestically generated price pressures are expected to pick up in the second half. Labour costs are set to rise along with growth in employment, while rental costs show signs of accelerating on the back of rising property prices in the first half of this year.
"As such, domestically generated inflation is likely to trend upward at a moderate pace, although this will be countered by subdued imported inflation," the bank said.
Hang Seng Bank said it expected export growth to rebound mildly in the second half in light of the economic recovery of Hong Kong's major export markets.
But a lacklustre performance in the first half meant that export growth for the full year would be much lower than the bank had originally forecast, it said.
The bank said it lowered its forecast for total export growth in 1997 to 4.6 percent from 9.7 percent.

The inflow of factor money -- income earned by Hong Kong investors and employees in other countries or territories -- which accounted for 35.7 percent of GDP in 1995, also is expected to benefit from the improved state of the world economy, Hang Seng Bank said.
Hang Seng Bank noted that the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development expects growth for OECD countries to average three percent in 1997, the highest rate since 1989.
The bank also predicted that building activities in Hong Kong would continue to accelerate, reflecting both private and public sector efforts to boost flat supply.
It projected that investment in plant and machinery would continue to grow at a steady clip.
